paragraphs.text: This [red tea](red:definition) was grown in Taiwan, the island off the coast of Fujian whose tea came across the strait with settlers. The label names [only the island](taiwan:on-a-label), with no mountain or township within it. Taiwan is known above all for oolong, but it [turned to red tea under Japanese rule](taiwan:history), and its first red tea was made at Yuchi, near Sun Moon Lake.

The leaf was made in 2023, so it is now three years old. [Red tea has no tradition of ageing](red:ageing). It is meant to be drunk fresh, and kept sealed it holds for about a year and a half to three years, so this tea is at the far end of that span.

English calls it black tea after the dark dry leaf, and Chinese calls it red after the colour of the cup. It is the fully oxidised tea. The fresh leaf is [withered](red:making) until it is soft enough to work, then rolled to break its cells, so that its juices and enzymes meet. It is left in warm, damp air until it turns from green to reddish brown, a step the Chinese trade calls fermentation. Hot air then dries it, which stops the change and keeps the tea stable.

brewing.text: Red tea takes water near the boil, about 90 to 100°C; hotter water draws out its aroma and flavour more fully, but its bitterness faster too. In a pot or mug, use about a rounded spoon of leaf for each cup and steep three to five minutes, less for broken leaf and a little less, and a little cooler, for a light, delicate tea. Left too long, it turns bitter and drying, because time and heat pull more tannins from the leaf.

notice.text: A sweet cup, often with honey, floral or fruity notes, malt in many, and a brisk strength in the stronger teas. The liquor runs red, bright to deep.
